title: Bien y Bueno: Practice
description: Authored B1 practice set for bien (adverb) vs bueno/buen/buena (adjective): which verbs each follows, the buen apocope before masculine nouns, estar bien vs ser bueno, and mejor covering both.

lessons.summary: Bien is an ADVERB: it describes how something is done, so it follows verbs: 'Cocinas bien', 'Dormí bien', 'Estoy bien'. It never changes form. Bueno is an ADJECTIVE: it describes a noun and agrees with it: 'una buena idea', 'un café bueno', 'unos días buenos'. Before a MASCULINE SINGULAR noun, bueno shortens to buen: 'un buen padre', 'buen provecho' (but 'una buena madre', no shortening in the feminine). The ser/estar pairing follows from that: estar bien = to be well/fine/OK (a state: health, mood, correctness), ser bueno = to be good (a quality: character, skill, 'ser bueno en algo'). Two extras worth drilling: with food, 'estar bueno/buena' means it tastes good right now ('¡Esta sopa está buena!'), while 'estar bien' means fine/enough ('Así está bien': that's enough). And the comparative of BOTH words is mejor: 'Cocinas mejor que yo' (never 'más bien'), 'Este café es mejor' (never 'más bueno').

examples.english: The baby slept well last night.
examples.note: bien after a verb: how he slept
bueno agreeing with a feminine noun
buen before a masculine singular noun

examples.english: Are you OK? You look tired.
You speak Spanish better than before.

items.explanation: Cocinar is a verb, and how you do a verb takes the adverb bien.
Idea is a feminine noun, so it takes the adjective buena (bien can't describe a noun).
Before a masculine singular noun, bueno drops the -o: un buen padre.

items.promptEnglish: The baby slept well last night.
items.explanation: Dormir is a verb: how he slept is the adverb bien.
Libro is a noun, so it needs the adjective. After the noun there's no shortening: un libro bueno.
Estar bien = to be well/fine. «Estoy bueno» means something quite different: that you find yourself attractive.

items.prompt: Mi vecina ___ muy buena: siempre nos ayuda.
items.promptEnglish: My neighbour is very good (kind). She always helps us.
items.explanation: Ser bueno/a = good as a quality of character. Estar buena would comment on her looks, not what you want to say about the neighbour.

items.prompt: ¡Probá la sopa! Está muy ___. (rica de sabor)
items.promptEnglish: Try the soup! It tastes really good.
items.explanation: With food, estar bueno/buena = it tastes good right now. Agrees with la sopa → buena.
Así está bien is the fixed way to say "that's fine / that's enough".

items.prompt: Hablas español ___ que el año pasado.
items.promptEnglish: You speak Spanish better than last year.
items.explanation: The comparative of bien is mejor: «más bien» and «más bueno» are the classic traps.

items.prompt: Este café es ___ que el del kiosco. (comparativo de bueno)
items.promptEnglish: This coffee is better than the one from the kiosk.
items.explanation: Bueno also uses mejor as its comparative, never «más bueno» in standard speech.
Provecho is masculine singular, so the shortened buen: ¡buen provecho! Same pattern as buen viaje, buen día.

items.prompt: Hoy Teo se portó muy ___ en el paseo. (bien / bueno)
items.promptEnglish: Teo behaved really well on the walk today.
items.explanation: Portarse bien = to behave well; behaving is a verb, so the adverb.
Noticia is feminine, so buena: the shortening to buen only happens before masculine singular nouns.
Oler is a verb, so how it smells is bien. English "smells good" pulls you toward the adjective, Spanish resists.

items.prompt: ¡Que tengas un ___ día! (forma corta de bueno)
items.explanation: Día is masculine (el día) even though it ends in -a, so it takes buen.

items.prompt: Lo pasamos muy ___ en la plaza.
items.promptEnglish: We had a really good time at the playground.
items.explanation: Pasarlo bien = to have a good time; a verb phrase, so the adverb.
